synopsis: A digital twin represents one specific real machine or site and promises agreement checked against measurements; neither the label nor a simulation package establishes credibility, which depends on the model, configuration, intended use and evidence [f13099, f13100, f7755]. The booklet recommends parameterised machine states and layered models per machine family rather than one ultimate twin, while machine geometry, self-occlusion and braking models can support coverage and blind-zone calculations before final hardware arrives [f1981, f6406, f13840, f5600, f5601]. This early modelling must not be presented as a validated sensor twin before hardware and mounting are frozen and correlated, and a team starting in October 2026 should not promise full multisensor, all-weather correlation by mid-2027 [f508, f871, f870]. For sites, exact copies and parameterised digital cousins serve complementary purposes, but no head-to-head perception or collision-avoidance comparison was found, reconstruction does not automatically yield simulation-ready truth, and no job-site twin price or person-day figures were found [f3751, f3752, f5104, f3903]. Evidence includes a physically calibrated AGX wheel-loader twin in 2025 and SynFog’s 2024 fog-chamber twin with matching simulated sensor trends, although SynFog is on-road evidence and existing construction-vehicle twins focused on dynamics and digging rather than perception [f8292, f4563, f468]. The only vendor off-road speed-up claim found was Robotec.ai/Boliden’s 30% faster validation cycles, but it concerns autonomous fleet behaviour rather than collision-intervention perception and lacks independent verification [f481, f482, f483].
